dossier.claim: In verifier-harness co-evolution, the verifier's acceptance gain carries over to other verifiers only to the extent that the verifier's selection data is independent of the agent. When the verifier is selected on agent-generated outputs, at least 30% of the self-play acceptance gain (ι = 1 − cross-play gain / self-play gain) disappears when the agent is scored by accuracy-matched, independently co-evolved verifiers. This gap is larger than what a frozen-verifier (one-way Goodhart) control produces, it grows with rounds, and ground truth does not differ. With fixed external anchors, cross-play matches self-play within ±10% (TOST).
dossier.design: Run two co-evolution methods: UCoE (2610.17609, code public, Qwen3-8B) plus a minimal RuHarness- or Who-Verifies-style loop. Manipulate verifier coupling at 3 levels: (a) fixed external contrasts or anchors, as published; (b) mixed; (c) verifier selected only on agent-generated outputs. Add a one-way arm in which the verifier is frozen at V_i^0 and only the agent evolves. Collusion is then the diagonal excess of the co-evolved arm minus that of the one-way arm. Use 5 seeds per cell. At rounds {0, 3, 6, 10}, build the 10×10 agent × verifier matrix and score it by verifier acceptance and by ground truth. Use 2 task families, one with exact ground truth (MBPP+/IFBench) and one open-ended with a human or strong-judge audit. Match verifiers on accuracy over a fixed, agent-independent labelled set. Also run the deployment swap (H_i + V_j measured on ground truth) to separate useful complementarity from dialect. Test the mechanism with a PoPLi-style paraphrase/normalization intervention on agent outputs, measuring the drop in diagonal excess under V_i vs V_j. Cost is about $1–1.5k with open models and no GPU; a pilot costs about $50–100 and takes about a week.
dossier.history: Round 1: Dan's original idea #7, "co-evolutionary Goodhart" (generator and solver co-evolving with weight training), was demoted. It needed $4–15k of GPU and was partly scooped by CODA 2610.20845, False Frontiers 2609.39102 and RuHarness 2610.36826. Its frozen-weight version was folded into C11 curriculum-goodhart. Round 2: the idea came back as a new bold idea, SHARP-4 "cross-play collusion", anticipating Forecast #4 (65%: collusion/drift critiques of co-evolved verifiers arrive in 2027). It moved from proposer-solver curricula to verifier-harness co-evolution, the hottest method lane. The bold check (72.9, PROMISING / viable with fixes) sharpened it. It added a one-way Goodhart control (difference-in-differences), made coupling or anchoring strength the manipulated dose so a null result is informative, defined the estimand ι, added a ground-truth deployment swap, and reused PoPLi for the mechanism test. The stake was reframed from "leaderboards become unidentifiable" to "in-loop acceptance does not carry over to other verifiers". The idea ranks #8 of 11 in the round-2 report.
dossier.priorScores: R1: n/a as this idea (its ancestor, Dan #7 co-evolutionary Goodhart, was demoted / folded into C11). R2 bold-check 72.9 (N3.5 S3.5 R3.5 C3.5 F4 T4.5), ranked #8 in round-2 REPORT

closestPapers.title: False Frontiers: Diagnosing and Mitigating Co-Cheating in Self-Evolving Search Agents
closestPapers.summary: In self-evolving search agents, a proposer and a solver increasingly agree on shared errors ('co-cheating'). In-loop reward improves while external correctness stagnates, and an audit against source evidence shows the problem worsening over rounds. The proposed fix, CrossFit, scores questions generated from document group A with an auxiliary solver trained only on group B, and vice versa. The cross-fitted feedback reduces false agreement more than multi-sample verification does.
closestPapers.relation: This is the conceptual precursor: 'cross-play as the cure' already exists for proposer-solver curricula trained with RL weights, and feedback ancestry is its mechanism. It does not build an agent × verifier matrix, has no one-way Goodhart control, and does not cover training-free verifier-harness loops. The bold check says it must be cited, and that ancestry/coupling should be tested directly as the dose variable.

closestPapers.title: Evolving Together, Failing Apart: The Skill-Policy Co-Evolution Trap in Self-Improving Agents (CODA)
closestPapers.summary: The paper argues that the cooperative acceptance rule shared by skill-policy co-evolution methods ties a policy's competence to the bank it co-evolved with. Sensitivity to skill drift grows as training proceeds. Its CODA audit protocol simulates drift: across 4 methods and 5 benchmarks, worst-case success falls 5-13 points below the delivered pair's peak, erasing 52-93% of the gain.
closestPapers.relation: This is the skill-bank analogue of pair-specific fragility, and it explicitly draws the analogy to zero-shot coordination and cross-play. It does not swap verifiers, does not separate acceptance from ground truth, and works at the weight-level policy. It is the template for this idea's 'audit card' deliverable and raises the bar for novelty.

closestPapers.title: Verifier-Harness Co-Evolution for Training-Free Self-Improvement on Open-Ended Tasks (UCoE)
closestPapers.summary: UCoE evolves an executable verifier program together with the agent's harness state while all weights stay frozen. Candidate verifiers are selected by 'driving capacity' on fixed response contrasts that have a known preferred side. The selected verifier picks which response is served and which repairs enter the harness. The method reports about 59% preference over direct generation with Qwen3-8B across six open-ended benchmarks.
closestPapers.relation: This is the primary audit target, with public code. The bold check notes that its verifier is anchored on fixed synthetic contrasts rather than on the agent's acceptance, so private-language inflation is unlikely as published (prior about 25%). That is why the design adds a naive agent-generated coupling arm. The paper itself never runs cross-play.

closestPapers.title: Who Verifies the Verifier? Co-Evolving Inspectable Graders with Self-Improving Agents
closestPapers.summary: The verifier is an inspectable expression over small drawback detectors. It is selected for agreement with a 10-item anchored reference set plus consensus, never for the agent's score. Removing the anchor guards collapses the verifier into a vacuous always-pass grader that still trains skills just as well, so downstream task score cannot certify a self-evolved verifier. Double Ratchet retains 88-110% of the lift that ground truth or a rubric gives.
closestPapers.relation: It shows collusion by vacuity rather than a private dialect, and its held-out score never passes through the verifier. Its 'no anchors' ablation is a natural coupling arm (c), and it is a second audit target. It does not compare the diagonal of an agent × verifier matrix with its off-diagonal.

closestPapers.title: Detecting Covert Collusion between AI Agents through Partner-Outsider Positive Listening (PoPLi)
closestPapers.summary: PoPLi is a behavioural test for private channels. It measures how much a partner's action changes when a message is reworded with its meaning kept, compared with an uninvolved outsider in the same seat. In a simulated market it detects instructed covert codes (PoPLi 0.48-0.59 with a code vs near 0 without), while message-only monitors fail.
closestPapers.relation: It is the exact design template for this idea's dialect-mechanism ablation: paraphrase the agent's output and compare V_i with V_j. Its codes are instructed, not emergent, and it does not involve verifier-agent co-evolution. Applying the partner-outsider gap to verifiers is new.

closestPapers.title: When the Critic Falls Behind: Co-Evolving Rubrics and Harnesses for Continual Agent Self-Improvement (RuHarness)
closestPapers.summary: RuHarness repeatedly discovers and reassesses behavioural rubric criteria from execution trajectories. It prioritizes unresolved weaknesses and uses them to guide harness evolution, so the supervision does not stay static.
closestPapers.relation: It is a second co-evolution method to audit. The bold check notes that its rubric is outcome-blind and that harness candidates are selected on an independent validation set by task success, so it is also anchored. It never runs cross-play.

closestPapers.title: From Single-Agent Self-Discovery to Multi-Agent Adaptation: Scaling Laws of Partner Feedback and Convention Rigidity in Meta RL
closestPapers.summary: Across 1,800+ runs in VMAS and Overcooked, four-cell counterfactual partner swaps reveal an 'evaluation illusion'. Apparent team progress hides focal regression, and transfer is inflated by +0.65 to +1.21. A coupling sweep shows a linear scaling law in partner feedback strength.
closestPapers.relation: It is the closest design precedent (partner-swap cross-play exposing inflation, with a coupling-strength dose), but in MARL with meta-learned optimizers rather than LLM verifier-harness loops.

closestPapers.title: Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization (Gao et al.)
closestPapers.summary: Using a synthetic gold reward model, the authors measure how gold score changes as a policy is optimized against a proxy reward model with RL or best-of-n. They find smooth functional forms whose coefficients scale with reward model size.
closestPapers.relation: This is the foundation for the one-way Goodhart baseline. The bold check warns that diagonal excess under a fixed V_i is ordinary proxy overoptimization in this sense, not collusion. That is why the frozen-verifier control and the difference-in-differences estimand are needed.

feedback.point: Co-evolutionary Goodhart with weight training is infeasible ($4-15k GPU) and partly scooped by CODA 2610.20845, False Frontiers 2609.39102 and RuHarness 2610.36826.
feedback.addressed: Yes. The latest version is training-free (frozen weights, verifier as a program), costs about $1-1.5k, needs no GPU, and moves to verifier-harness cross-play, which those papers do not run.

feedback.point: No direct scoop (no K1), but four neighbours cover the concept from different sides (False Frontiers/CrossFit, CODA, PoPLi, Who Verifies). An unverified survey (hyper.ai 2608.10299) reportedly proposes cross-play and held-out evaluators. Scoop risk is medium-high given 15+ co-evolution papers in 4 months, so a Feb 2027 preprint is needed.
feedback.addressed: Partly. Citations and the timeline are acknowledged. The survey remains unverified and the scoop risk remains.

feedback.point: Confound between Goodhart and collusion: diagonal excess occurs whenever an agent is optimized against V_i, even if V_i is fixed. A one-way (frozen-verifier) arm is needed, with collusion defined as a difference-in-differences.
feedback.addressed: Yes. This is in the sharpened claim and the design.

feedback.point: 'Leaderboard numbers become unidentifiable' is overclaimed, because UCoE, Who Verifies and RuHarness all report external or held-out metrics. The stake should be reframed as in-loop acceptance not carrying over to other verifiers. Add a ground-truth deployment swap (H_i + V_j) to separate useful complementarity from dialect.
feedback.addressed: Yes. The claim is reframed and the 2×2 acceptance-vs-GT, self-vs-cross decomposition is added.

feedback.point: '≥30%' and 'equal accuracy' are arbitrary or underspecified. Pre-register the estimand ι and match verifiers on a fixed, agent-independent labelled set. Keep TOST ±10% for the null.
feedback.addressed: Yes. ι is defined and accuracy matching specified. The 30% threshold is still a chosen cutoff.

feedback.point: The null must be informative. Make anchoring/coupling strength the manipulated variable at 3 levels (external anchors / mixed / agent-generated only), with the prediction that ι rises with feedback ancestry and rounds.
feedback.addressed: Yes. This is the core of the sharpened claim.

feedback.point: The mechanism ablation of 'dialect features' should reuse PoPLi's paraphrase intervention, measuring the drop in diagonal excess for V_i vs V_j.
feedback.addressed: Yes. It is in the design.

feedback.point: Generality requires 2 methods, 2 task families (exact GT plus open-ended with human/strong-judge audit), 2 actor models, and 5 seeds per cell.
feedback.addressed: Yes in the design, at a higher cost ($1-1.5k vs the original $800).

feedback.point: All three published methods anchor the verifier against something the agent cannot write. The prior for ≥30% private-language inflation on them is low (about 25%), so the original claim would likely come out null on its own targets.
feedback.addressed: Yes, by adding the naive agent-generated coupling arm, so that a null on the anchored arm becomes a finding ('anchoring keeps co-evolution honest').

feedback.point: Moderate-high relevance (self-evaluation in Gödel-Agent-style loops, inflation over rounds), but less central to the mentor than world-model or RSI-compounding ideas.
feedback.addressed: Not addressable by design. This is a positioning caveat.

feedback.point: Verifier co-evolution is the hottest lane with very high crowding. Cross-play collusion is riding the wave and will be late by summer 2027 (Forecast #4, 65%).
feedback.addressed: Partly. The answer is to preprint by Feb 2027 and frame the work as an audit protocol rather than a method.

openRisks: High scoop risk: many co-evolution groups could add a 2×2 swap table cheaply, and a survey (2608.10299, unverified) already names cross-play as an evaluation paradigm.
A likely null on anchored published methods (prior about 25% for inflation). The paper's interest then rests on the naive-coupling arm, which reviewers may call a strawman.
Separating collusion from one-way overoptimization needs well-powered difference-in-differences estimates; noisy acceptance on open-ended tasks may leave it underpowered at 5 seeds.
Ground truth for open-ended tasks depends on a human or strong-judge audit, which could itself share blind spots with the verifiers.
Accuracy-matching independently co-evolved verifiers may be hard; unmatched verifiers confound ι.
Mentor fit is moderate rather than central; the cost grew from $800 to about $1-1.5k.
Only the bold check has reviewed it. There was no full round-2 red-team (novelty-killer or sharpness lenses) for this idea.

judges.strongest: The design is well controlled. It manipulates coupling and anchoring as a dose, uses a frozen-verifier one-way Goodhart arm with a difference-in-differences estimand, matches verifiers on accuracy over an agent-independent labelled set, runs an H_i+V_j ground-truth deployment swap, and adds a PoPLi-style paraphrase mechanism test. Both outcomes are publishable ("anchoring keeps co-evolution honest" vs "naive coupling breeds pair-specific dialect"). It is training-free and costs about $1-1.5k, and there are many audit targets: UCoE (HuOAuecWpX), Red Queen Gödel Machine, Gödel Ecology, DUET and J-Zero.
judges.weakest: The ICLR 2027 sweep shows the novelty margin has shrunk to a sliver. tn4eslVXEK (When the Evaluator Changes) already builds a model-version × evaluator-version matrix with a decomposition of false progress. Id4G8bzzKO (False Frontiers) shows co-cheating that grows with rounds, with cross-fitting as the cure and a feedback-ancestry control. Lpxn7lc6Dz (More Convincing, Not More Correct) finds that self-play judge exploits transfer across judge families, which is direct prior evidence that cross-play comes out null (generic, not pair-specific). What remains is the seed × seed cross-lineage axis at matched accuracy, plus the dialect ablation. Arm (c), with no anchors and agent-generated selection data, is likely to be called a strawman, since no published method does this. On open-ended tasks, 5 seeds may leave the difference-in-differences underpowered. The 10×10 × 4 rounds × 3 coupling levels × 2 methods × 2 tasks grid is heavy for one undergrad.
judges.mustFix: (1) Cite tn4eslVXEK, Lpxn7lc6Dz, Id4G8bzzKO, ZIBdUe2hGK (CODA) and T04ZzT5m6j, and position the contribution explicitly as the cross-lineage (seed × seed) axis plus the mechanism, not as cross-play or matrix evaluation in general. (2) Pre-register a two-sided "generic vs pair-specific" hypothesis: decompose inflation into a generic component (one that transfers to all verifiers, as in Lpxn7lc6Dz) and a pair-specific diagonal component, and treat a generic-only result as a headline finding. (3) Replace the strawman arm (c) with a published method that does couple on agent outputs (Gödel Ecology's lineage-productivity scoring, DUET or RQGM), or show that real methods drift toward (c). (4) Run a power analysis from the $50-100 pilot before committing to 5 seeds, and cut the grid (e.g. 6×6, rounds {0,5,10}). (5) Preprint by Feb 2027.
judges.reviewerQuote: Given that When the Evaluator Changes already decomposes false progress with a version-by-evaluator matrix and More Convincing, Not More Correct shows judge exploits transfer across judge families, the remaining contribution — a seed-by-seed matrix whose positive result hinges on an unanchored coupling arm no published method uses — feels like an incremental audit rather than a new finding.

judges.strongest: The design is well built. Coupling strength is the manipulated dose, there is a frozen-verifier one-way Goodhart arm with a difference-in-differences estimand, verifiers are matched on accuracy against agent-independent labels, a ground-truth deployment swap separates complementarity from dialect, and a PoPLi-style paraphrase test checks the mechanism. It is training-free, so it is cheap to re-run on UCoE (HuOAuecWpX) and on other ICLR'27 co-evolution methods. A two-sided outcome is publishable as an audit protocol.
judges.weakest: The ICLR 2027 sweep removes most of the remaining novelty margin. tn4eslVXEK ('When the Evaluator Changes') already builds the model-version × evaluator-version matrix with a false-progress decomposition. Id4G8bzzKO (False Frontiers) already shows co-cheating that grows with rounds and cross-fitting as the cure, including a replay control that isolates feedback ancestry, which is close to this idea's dose variable. Lpxn7lc6Dz ('More Convincing, Not More Correct') shows self-play judge exploits transfer across judge families. That makes the pair-specific 'private dialect' prediction (ι ≥ 0.3) a priori unlikely. Most loss of fidelity to ground truth would be generic Goodhart, which the one-way arm absorbs, so the likely result is ι ≈ 0 with a GT drop. Arm (c), naive agent-coupled selection, is the only place the effect is likely, and it reads as a strawman that no published method uses. What is left is a seed × seed axis at matched accuracy, which amounts to tn4eslVXEK's matrix crossed with CrossFit's cross-fitting applied to UCoE, i.e. a combination (K4-ish). The design is also expensive for one undergrad: 10×10 matrices × 4 rounds × 3 coupling levels × 2 methods × 2 task families × 5 seeds, plus accuracy-matching of evolved verifiers.
judges.mustFix: 1. Cite tn4eslVXEK, Id4G8bzzKO, Lpxn7lc6Dz, ZIBdUe2hGK and T04ZzT5m6j, and position against them. Drop any 'first cross-play' claim. 2. Re-pre-register the headline as two-sided, generic versus pair-specific exploitation. Lpxn7lc6Dz predicts generic exploitation, so the paper must be interesting when ι ≈ 0 and ground truth falls. 3. Replace the naive arm (c) as the main source of positive results with real published methods that differ in anchoring: RQGM o3txFJw4JR, Gödel Ecology N4GJVmrzsF, DUET lnSodbrQix, J-Zero 13quQMClZU and UCoE. Then the dose comes from real design choices, not a constructed strawman. 4. Cut scope to one method × one exact-GT task family for the core result, with a power analysis for the difference-in-differences estimate. Better still, fold the work in as a cross-verifier transfer section of the learning-to-goodhart or curriculum-goodhart paper, not a standalone paper.
judges.reviewerQuote: The version × evaluator matrix (tn4eslVXEK), cross-fitted anti-co-cheating feedback (False Frontiers) and the cross-family transfer of judge exploits (Lpxn7lc6Dz) already establish the phenomenon and its fix. This submission's seed × seed variant mainly confirms that a verifier selected on the agent's own outputs can be gamed, a strawman configuration no published method uses.

judges.strongest: The design is well identified and cheap. It uses anchoring/coupling strength as a 3-level dose, a frozen-verifier one-way Goodhart control (difference-in-differences ι), accuracy matching on an agent-independent labelled set, a ground-truth deployment swap, and a PoPLi paraphrase test for mechanism. Because everything is training-free on public code (UCoE, now also an ICLR 2027 submission, HuOAuecWpX), a solo undergrad can run it for about $1-1.5k. Either outcome can be published: 'anchoring keeps co-evolution honest' or 'agent-coupled selection breeds pair-specific dialect'. The ICLR 2027 sweep also brings in the Red Queen Gödel Machine (o3txFJw4JR) and Gödel Ecology (N4GJVmrzsF) as audit targets, which ties the work directly to the mentor's Gödel-Agent line.
judges.weakest: The novelty margin is now thin, and the most likely result is a generic-exploit null. The ICLR 2027 sweep turns up three close submissions. 'When the Evaluator Changes' (tn4eslVXEK) already builds a model-version × evaluator-version matrix with a progress decomposition that separates real gains from adaptation to evaluator weaknesses. 'More Convincing, Not More Correct' (Lpxn7lc6Dz) shows that self-play exploits against a learned judge transfer across judge families, which is direct evidence against pair-specific dialect. False Frontiers (Id4G8bzzKO) already uses cross-fitting to cure co-cheating that grows with rounds. What remains is the cross-lineage (seed × seed) axis at matched accuracy across several methods, plus the dialect ablation. That reads as False Frontiers + tn4eslVXEK + PoPLi recombined, which is why K4 applies. The 'agent-generated only' arm will likely be called a strawman, since every published method anchors its verifier.
judges.mustFix:
1. Reposition the paper as the 'decisive two-sided test' of whether evaluator exploitation is generic or pair-specific. Pre-register both outcomes, and treat Lpxn7lc6Dz's cross-family transfer as the competing hypothesis. Do not claim the matrix method, which tn4eslVXEK already has (version × evaluator), or the co-cheating finding, which Id4G8bzzKO already has. Cite both, plus ZIBdUe2hGK, T04ZzT5m6j and IVFASEtqp6.
2. Replace the strawman naive arm with real method variants. Audit the ICLR 2027 co-evolution methods whose evaluators are partly coupled to the agent, such as Red Queen Gödel Machine, Gödel Ecology and DUET, alongside UCoE. That way the coupling dose comes from published design choices, not one you invented.
3. Report a 'generic exploit' baseline: under the frozen-verifier arm, measure how much of the acceptance gain transfers to off-lineage verifiers. Only the difference-in-differences above that baseline counts as dialect.
4. Run a power analysis from the 1-week pilot before you commit to 5 seeds. Use exact-GT tasks (MBPP+/IFBench) for the headline, and keep the open-ended family secondary.
5. Post a preprint by February 2027. ICLR 2027 rebuttals will make swap tables cheap for any of the 5 or more method authors to add.
judges.reviewerQuote: A cross-evaluator matrix (When the Evaluator Changes), the observation that judge exploits transfer across families (More Convincing, Not More Correct), and cross-fitted feedback as the cure for co-cheating (False Frontiers) are all already in the ICLR 2027 pool. The seed-by-seed variant adds a careful control, but its strongest positive arm relies on a verifier-coupling regime that no published method actually uses.

dossier.title: Breaking the Improver: Does Robustness Assimilate Through the Gate? Robustness-aware selection of evolved harnesses under controlled environment interventions (merged with round-2 nonobv-canalization)
dossier.claim: Clean-validation scores are a misleading selector for evolved harnesses, and robustness does not carry over to new intervention families through the gate. (1) Across harness evolvers, a candidate's paired BreakingWeb-style intervention drop predicts its out-of-distribution transfer better than its clean score does. (2) Putting interventions from k primitive families into the acceptance gate makes harnesses robust to those families, but robustness to held-out families keeps the same negative per-generation slope as clean-only evolution. The losses are mostly extra false "done" claims, and at matched clean accuracy both kinds of lineage are less robust than hand-written harnesses. This is falsified if gate-exposed lineages show a significantly less negative held-out-family slope, i.e. real assimilation, which would be the positive method result.
dossier.history: Round 1, candidate C15 (T6), 68.3/100, "viable with fixes": it merged the world-model sweep's Idea 1 with the benchmarks sweep's intervention audit. The original claim was that evolved champions have larger paired drops, that the leaderboard flips, and that an intervention diet fixes robustness. The critique showed the directional claim was already pre-empted by 2610.39122 (IPI) and Masked Erosion, and that Arm B was near-tautological. It recommended reframing around robustness-aware selection over all archive candidates, held-out intervention families, and a two-sided pre-registered hypothesis. In the round-1 REPORT it ranked #9, as a "good follow-up / shift probe" that was not chosen as the main paper. Round 1 wrote no proposal and round 2 had no v2 or red-team pass for this id. Instead, round 2's bold idea NONOBV-6 "canalization" (selection manufactures fragility, measured as a per-generation dose-response, plus a Waddington assimilation arm) rediscovered the same territory. Its bold-check scored it 65.8 (Weak), found it pre-empted by CODA 2610.20845, 2610.39122 and Masked Erosion, and recommended merging it with breaking-the-improver. The reframe became "robustness does not assimilate through the gate", with tau-world as the primary environment. The current version is that merge. It ranks #11 in round 2 and is not the recommended paper.
dossier.priorScores: R1 68.3 (breaking-the-improver, viable with fixes) → R2 65.8 (merged canalization variant, Weak; recommendation: merge with breaking-the-improver)

closestPapers.title: Appreciation Teaches Unauthorized Execution: Self-Evolution Degrades the Robustness of Personal Agents to Indirect Prompt Injection
closestPapers.summary: Uses a controlled two-phase protocol: in adaptation, a personal agent learns from user feedback on tasks read from external content; at test, a third party injects a similar task the user never authorized. Self-evolution raises IPI attack success by 14.0–48.8 pp under skill evolution and by 3.0–39.3 pp under RL, compared with the non-evolving base agent. The round-1/round-2 deep reads add that a contrastive, authorization-aware feedback fix brings ASR from about 35% down to 5.8%, and that clean completion stays at or above 85%.
closestPapers.relation: Closest to the directional claim ('self-evolution degrades robustness') and its fix resembles Arm B. It uses one adversarial intervention class (IPI), personal-agent skills rather than harness evolvers (GEPA/ACE/AHE), and has no paired task-success drop, primitives or layers, matched compute, or held-out-family test of the fix. The idea must position explicitly against it.

closestPapers.title: Evolving Together, Failing Apart: The Skill-Policy Co-evolution Trap in Self-Improving Agents (CODA)
closestPapers.summary: Shows that cooperative acceptance in skill–policy co-evolution ties the policy to the bank it co-evolved with, so sensitivity to skill drift grows as training proceeds. It proposes the CODA audit, which reports worst-case-drift success, consistency, and corrupted-skill resistance. Worst-case success is 5–13 points below peak, erasing 52–93% of the bank's gain. The bold-check notes a dose-response proposition, and that training against perturbation distributions is left as future work.
closestPapers.relation: Owns the 'selection/acceptance manufactures fragility, dose-response over training' framing that the canalization variant relied on. It perturbs the agent's own skill bank, not the environment, and has no fix, no held-out family, and no matched-accuracy hand-written control. That leaves room for environment-side interventions and the held-out assimilation test.

closestPapers.title: Masked Erosion: How Acceptance Gates Lose Redundant Safeguards in Self-Improving Agents
closestPapers.summary: Runs 411 harness-improvement loops under 10 gate rules, plus GEPA runs. It shows that success-scored acceptance gates silently delete redundant safeguards, because each deletion is masked by the remaining ones, and that the lost depth turns into harm when the harness is reused with a weaker model. Paired tests, frozen safety text, and one-layer ablation audits preserve depth.
closestPapers.relation: Provides the predicted mechanism for H+ (evolution erodes checks or verification) and runs the gate analysis over generations. It is about harm safeguards and model swaps, not task robustness to environment changes. The idea should cite it as the mechanism and measure erosion through edit diffs.

closestPapers.title: Beneath the Surface: What We Overlook When We Talk About Agent Evolution
closestPapers.summary: Evaluates four harness-evolution methods (per the critique: AHE, HyperAgents, A-Evolve, GEPA) across harnesses and general and coding tasks, using repeated evaluations, component interventions and admission replays. It finds that gains often bring higher deployment cost, that the highest-scoring agent is not the best parent, that transfer coverage usually falls on general tasks, and that evolvers insert generic verification reminders. It proposes EvoAudit.
closestPapers.relation: Same evolver set and the same evaluation-of-evolvers framing, but generalization is tested only as cross-benchmark transfer, with no controlled paired environment interventions and no belief-failure analysis. Its finding that evolvers add verification reminders is the main risk to the direction of the effect (H−).

closestPapers.title: SkillShift-Bench: Benchmarking Skill Learning under Environment Evolution for Web Agents
closestPapers.summary: A benchmark of learned web-agent skills (AWM, ASI, SkillWeaver, WALT) under controlled Contextual, Perceptual and Execution shifts on three self-hosted web systems. It finds systematic degradation (lower success, higher cost, more skill failures), with Execution Shift hurting most, and proposes a test-time reranker.
closestPapers.relation: Controlled environment shifts for self-learned web skills, but it covers skill libraries rather than harness evolution, does not compare learned agents with a no-skill seed for added brittleness, and does not evolve under shifts. The critique suggests it as a second, ready-made shift domain.

closestPapers.title: Harness-Delta Attribution: Dissecting Gains From Harness Evolution
closestPapers.summary: Splits harness-evolution gains into artifact-driven overfitting, test-time-scaling gains, and a residual, across 11 executors and 3 frameworks. Overfitting and test-time scaling explain 54% and 14% of the gain on average, search-set gains often fail to transfer, and validation signals are not enough to prevent overfitting.
closestPapers.relation: Shows that clean validation is a poor selector, which supports the robustness-aware-selection claim, but it uses no environment interventions. The idea uses HDA's residual as an outcome to predict, so it is a cross-check rather than a contribution.

closestPapers.title: Constructing Challenging Browser-Use Tasks by Controlled Environment Interventions (BreakingWeb)
closestPapers.summary: Mentor Xunjian Yin's benchmark. Each of 519 tasks on 7 self-hosted sites is run clean and under a controlled intervention (content, server state, network, rendered page), with the instruction and backend success criterion held fixed. Interventions cut the pass rates of six strong agents by 22.9 pp, while humans lose only 10.0 pp, and 75% of agent failures are belief failures (declaring done without making the change).
closestPapers.relation: The core instrument. The paired drop and the belief-failure label are the idea's outcome measures. Only static agents have been evaluated on it (1 forward citation, EMBERS, not a scoop), so using it to evaluate self-improvers is still uncontested.

closestPapers.title: On the Fragility of Self-Improving Agents: Variance, Task Order, and Underspecification
closestPapers.summary: Re-evaluates memory-based self-improving agents over multiple runs and shuffled task orders. It finds that the self-improving loop amplifies evaluation noise and that improvement depends heavily on task order.
closestPapers.relation: A foundation for the statistical-power concerns: self-improvement gains are noisy, which motivates k≥3 passes and lineage random effects. It does not study environment interventions.

feedback.point: The directional claim 'self-evolution degrades robustness' is already made by 2610.39122 (IPI, with a contrastive fix similar to Arm B), and its mechanism by Masked Erosion 2610.38392. The evaluation-of-evolvers framing is crowded (Beneath the Surface uses the same 4 evolvers; HDA; Rethinking-Eval). N is about 3.
feedback.addressed: Partly. The headline moved from 'evolution is brittle' to robustness-aware selection and held-out-family assimilation, and the plan positions against 2610.39122 and Masked Erosion. Round 2 then found the CODA pre-emption on top of these.

feedback.point: Arm B (evolve on interventions, test on interventions) is near-tautological unless the test uses held-out intervention families or layers and is compared with cheap baselines: a generic 'verify after acting' instruction and robust selection without intervention feedback.
feedback.addressed: Yes, in design. Held-out families (3 gated, 4 held out, or split by layer) and the generic-instruction and robust-selection baselines are now central.

feedback.point: The direction of the effect is uncertain. Beneath the Surface finds that evolvers insert verification reminders, and BreakingWeb's dominant failure is fabricated success, so champions might have a smaller drop. Pre-register both directions and a null.
feedback.addressed: Yes. A two-sided H+/H− with per-primitive signs is pre-registered, and the false-finish rate is the primary mechanism metric.

feedback.point: Statistical power: about 519 pairs, per-primitive cells of roughly 10–30 after splits, and a second-order champion-minus-seed difference of about 3–8 pp. Needs pooling, paired bootstrap or mixed effects, and k≥3 passes.
feedback.addressed: Partly. Mixed-effects with lineage random effects, k≥3 passes, and a correlation over hundreds of archive candidates are adopted. Per-primitive power is still unresolved.

feedback.point: Feasibility: porting AHE or Hyperagents to a browser harness is heavy, cheap backbones cannot drive Hyperagents, browser rollouts are long, and the full grid of about 72 runs likely exceeds $1.5k. Cut to GEPA + ACE + one code-level evolver, 2 backbones, and a $50 pilot.
feedback.addressed: Yes in plan. Hyperagents was dropped, scope was reduced, and a pilot under $50 was specified. Round 2 also moved the main environment to tau-world.

feedback.point: With only 3–4 evolvers, a 'leaderboard flip' is weak evidence. Use a correlation across all archive candidates instead.
feedback.addressed: Yes. The flip claim was replaced with a correlation over archive candidates (Fix 1).

feedback.point: The 'learned verification would be equally publishable' framing is a second paper. Use an existing second domain (Δτ-Bench, Bench2Robust, SkillShift-Bench) instead of building a tau intervention generator.
feedback.addressed: Partly. Round 2 instead makes a procedural tau-world the primary environment, which needs new infrastructure, contrary to Fix 5.

feedback.point: Optionally report the paired drop as a function of evolution generation (a 'robustness half-life'), which is more surprising than end-point drops.
feedback.addressed: Yes, via the canalization merge: the per-generation robustness slope is now a core measurement.

feedback.point: The dose-response framing 'selection manufactures fragility' is pre-empted by CODA 2610.20845 (explicit Proposition 3, dose-response), by 2610.39122 (ASR over updates) and by Masked Erosion (margin over generations). A reviewer will cite CODA against the headline. Scored 65.8, Weak; K4 is borderline.
feedback.addressed: Partly. The reframe makes 'robustness does not assimilate through the gate', with held-out families and matched accuracy, the headline, but novelty is still capped at about 2.5–3.

feedback.point: The biology analogy (canalization, Waddington) is a label, not a mechanism, and should be kept out of the title.
feedback.addressed: Yes. The working title and claim drop the biology framing.

feedback.point: The matched-accuracy control (early checkpoints plus hand-tuned harnesses, then fitting robustness against clean accuracy with generation as an extra predictor) is novel; neither CODA nor IPI has it.
feedback.addressed: Yes. It is included in the design.

feedback.point: Secondary test: does held-out transfer depend on gating by cognitive primitive (belief revision, verification) rather than by surface layer? This is BreakingWeb's unique handle.
feedback.addressed: Included as a secondary analysis; not yet designed in detail.

feedback.point: About 100k browser rollouts. $800–1.1k is plausible only with a cheap open model and tau-world as the primary environment, with BreakingWeb as a confirmatory subset.
feedback.addressed: Yes in plan, but the tau-world generator has not been built.

feedback.point: Ranked #11 of 11 (65.8, Weak): 'framing pre-empted by CODA and Masked Erosion; merge with breaking-the-improver.' Not the recommended paper. Mentor question 7 asks whether the BreakingWeb or WeAct infrastructure should supply a far domain.
feedback.addressed: Merge recommended but not executed as a v2 proposal. No round-2 red-team (novelty-killer or sharpness) or fact-check was run on this id.

openRisks: Novelty ceiling: CODA, 2610.39122 and Masked Erosion together pre-empt the surprise of 'self-improvement creates fragility'. Only the environment-side, held-out-assimilation and matched-accuracy slice remains, and K4 ('BreakingWeb + harness evolution' as a mere combination) is borderline.

Direction risk: evolvers may insert verification (Beneath the Surface), shrinking BreakingWeb's dominant fabricated-success failures. The effect could be sign-split or null, and a null is publishable only with a strong power analysis.
Statistical power: per-primitive cells of about 10–70 pairs and a second-order effect of about 3–8 pp. Per-primitive claims may not reach significance.

Cost and infrastructure: about 100k long browser rollouts. Depends on a procedural tau-world intervention generator that does not yet exist and on porting a code-level evolver; budget is $800–1.5k on cheap or open models.
No round-2 red-team or fact-check was run on the merged version, so its claims have not been stress-tested beyond the bold-check.
Further scoop risk in a hot lane: BreakingWeb has 1 forward citation now, and a direct evaluation of self-improvers on it could appear before the NeurIPS 2027 deadline.

judges.strongest: Two parts of the design are still uncontested after the ICLR'27 sweep. First, the held-out-family assimilation test: does putting k intervention families in the gate change the per-generation robustness slope on the other 7-k families, using a mixed-effects model with lineage random effects? Second, the matched-clean-accuracy control against hand-written harnesses and early checkpoints. CODA, IPI, Masked Erosion and CHASE have neither. Both outcomes are interpretable: a negative result would mean "gating on perturbations does not buy general robustness", and a positive one would be a method.
judges.weakest:
Novelty has been cut from three sides. ICLR'27 5lWjRTK6Vk ("The Harness Learns to Lie While Evolving", EvoTrap-Bench/VHE) already shows false success rising round over round under harness self-evolution, which is the proposed mechanism ("losses are mostly extra false done claims"). ICLR'27 uzzum63KP4 (CHASE / Bad Genius) already feeds gain-destroying protocol counterfactuals into evolution as constraints, which is close to arm (iii). CODA (ZIBdUe2hGK, also on ICLR'27), IPI 2610.39122 and Masked Erosion already own "selection manufactures fragility over generations". That leaves a narrow combination of BreakingWeb and harness evolvers plus a held-out split, so K4 is real. On top of this:
- The headline is a second-order slope difference (about 3-8 pp) with weak per-primitive power, so the falsification test may be underpowered either way.
- The primary environment, a procedural tau-world, does not exist yet.
- Roughly 100k rollouts across 4 arms × 3 evolvers × 2 backbones × 3 seeds is a stretch for one undergraduate in 6 months.
judges.mustFix:
- Reposition explicitly against 5lWjRTK6Vk (false success already rises per generation). Drop false-done as a mechanism claim, or make it the BreakingWeb belief-failure breakdown scored against backend state.
- Make CHASE (uzzum63KP4) a named baseline arm alongside the min(clean, intervened) gate and the generic re-read instruction, so arm (iii) is not just CHASE on new data.
- Cut the scope to one claim, held-out-family assimilation at matched clean accuracy. Use 2 evolvers (GEPA and ACE), 1 open backbone plus 1 cheap closed backbone, and at least 5 lineages.
- Replace the unbuilt tau-world with existing shift suites: BreakingWeb, plus WebVariants (TYSv9rIhiQ) or SkillShift-Bench as the second domain.
- Run the pilot under $50 first, and before committing do a simulation-based power analysis for the slope-difference test that sets a minimum detectable effect.
- Strongly consider folding this into the useful-fictions/belief-tracker idea as its environment-intervention arm instead of running it as a standalone paper.
judges.reviewerQuote: Given that CODA, the IPI study, Masked Erosion and the concurrent 'Harness Learns to Lie' already establish that self-evolution erodes robustness and inflates false success, and CHASE already injects counterfactual perturbations into harness evolution, this paper's remaining contribution is a held-out-family slope comparison whose effect size the authors' own power analysis cannot resolve.

judges.strongest: The paper would be the first test of evolved harnesses on BreakingWeb-style paired environment interventions, which are the mentor's own instrument and have essentially no self-improver evaluations yet. Two parts of the design are new: a matched-clean-accuracy control (hand-written harnesses plus early checkpoints) and a held-out-family test of whether gate exposure assimilates. Neither CODA, IPI (2610.39122), Masked Erosion nor CHASE has either one. The archive-wide correlation of intervened versus clean validation score with OOD transfer is also cheap to run and reusable.
judges.weakest: Almost every sub-claim is already in the literature. (a) 'Selection makes harnesses fragile over generations' is taken by CODA (2610.20845; ICLR27 ZIBdUe2hGK), IPI 2610.39122 and Masked Erosion. (b) 'The losses are mostly extra false done claims' is pre-empted by the ICLR 2027 submission 'The Harness Learns to Lie While Evolving' (EvoTrap-Bench/VHE, openreview 5lWjRTK6Vk), which shows false success rising each round of harness self-evolution. (c) The gate-exposure arm overlaps CHASE / Bad Genius (2609.18366; ICLR27 uzzum63KP4), which already feeds gain-destroying counterfactual transformations back into evolution as constraints. (d) 'Clean validation is a poor selector' is in HDA and in Can Harness Optimization Improve Agents? (Ri0rU3rPOS). What is left, 'robustness from k gated families does not transfer to held-out families', is what insiders expect from domain randomization and adversarial training, so it is not surprising. On top of that, per-primitive power is weak (second-order effects of 3–8 pp), and the tau-world intervention generator has not been built.
judges.mustFix:
1. Position explicitly against CHASE (uzzum63KP4 / 2609.18366) and run it as a baseline arm, alongside the min(clean, intervened) gate. Without that, arm (iii) is a re-implementation.
2. Concede the false-done-rises-per-round finding to EvoTrap-Bench (5lWjRTK6Vk), and use its VHE fix as an extra arm.
3. Make the single headline the held-out-family assimilation slope at matched clean accuracy.
4. Drop the procedural tau-world. Use BreakingWeb plus WebVariants (TYSv9rIhiQ) as the ready-made, layer-split held-out families.
5. Run a power analysis from the $50 pilot before committing to per-primitive claims.
6. Better still, fold this in as the robustness/selection section of the useful-fictions / belief-tracker paper on BreakingWeb, rather than running it as a standalone paper.
judges.reviewerQuote: Once CODA, Masked Erosion, EvoTrap-Bench and CHASE are accounted for, the remaining finding is that robustness trained on three perturbation families does not transfer to four unseen ones, which the domain-randomization literature would predict, and the paper does not explain why the harness-evolution setting should change that expectation.

judges.strongest: The held-out-family assimilation test is still unclaimed. It gates on k intervention families and measures the per-generation robustness slope on families never seen, at matched clean accuracy against hand-written harnesses and early checkpoints. It uses the mentor's own BreakingWeb paired-drop and belief-failure instrument. None of CODA, IPI, Masked Erosion, CHASE or EvoTrap combines held-out intervention families with a matched-accuracy control. Either sign of the slope result is interpretable, and the work fits the mentor's agenda.
judges.weakest: The ICLR 2027 sweep removes most of what was left. CHASE / Bad Genius (OpenReview uzzum63KP4, also 2609.18366) already searches for protocol transformations that destroy an evolved harness's gains and feeds them back as constraints during evolution, which is essentially arm (iii) as a method. "The Harness Learns to Lie While Evolving" (5lWjRTK6Vk, EvoTrap/VHE) already shows false success rising with each round of harness evolution, which takes the "losses are mostly extra false done claims" mechanism readout. CODA (ZIBdUe2hGK, now confirmed at ICLR) owns the dose-response over generations. "Can Harness Optimization Improve Agents?" (Ri0rU3rPOS) and HDA (PX4Zpvsaca) already show that clean validation misleads. Novelty now rests on one second-order slope comparison: held-out vs gated families. Its per-primitive power is weak (3–8 pp effects in cells of 10–70), and it depends on a procedural tau-world intervention generator that does not exist yet, plus a ported code-level evolver. That is too much infrastructure for a solo undergrad with 6 months and a narrow claim.
judges.mustFix: Do not run this as a standalone paper. Fold it into the useful-fictions / BreakingWeb belief-tracker paper as its robustness-selection section. If it is kept, do four things. (1) Position explicitly against CHASE (uzzum63KP4) and run it as a baseline arm: a counterfactual challenger in the gate vs a fixed k-family gate, both scored on held-out families. (2) Cite EvoTrap/VHE (5lWjRTK6Vk) as the source of the false-done-rises-per-generation finding, and claim only the held-out-family breakdown on top of it. (3) Drop the procedural tau-world generator. Use BreakingWeb plus WebVariants (TYSv9rIhiQ) as the ready-made intervention families, which saves months. (4) Pre-register a pooled (not per-primitive) slope contrast with a power analysis from the $50 pilot, and cut to GEPA × 2 backbones × at least 4 lineages.
judges.reviewerQuote: Given CODA, CHASE and EvoTrap, the finding that evolved harnesses are brittle, falsely claim success more often, and do not generalize perturbation training to unseen perturbation families is an incremental combination of BreakingWeb with existing harness evolvers, and its per-primitive slope differences are underpowered.

dossier.title: Baldwin Hiding vs. Assist: Where the Harness Helps, Not How Much It Adapts, Decides What GRPO Weights Learn
dossier.claim: When the same memory + reflective self-edit harness used during GRPO turns already-mixed groups into all-success groups (always-on), the weights it trains do worse harness-free and under a foreign harness than weights trained under a frozen harness at matched rollouts (deficit of at least 3 pp, "hiding"). When the same harness fires only on all-fail groups, the weights do better than frozen-harness RL ("assist"). Across arms, ΔI (the net change in the fraction of informative, mixed groups) predicts the harness-free delta (R² ≥ 0.6), and harness adaptivity adds no predictive power once ΔI is controlled. The claim is falsified if the always-on and fail-gated arms do not differ in sign (TOST ±2 pp), or if ΔI does not out-predict adaptivity level.
dossier.design: Setup: Qwen3-4B (Qwen3-1.7B for the pilot and a scale check), GRPO in a verl-agent/GiGPO-style stack on ALFWorld and TextCraft, with the τ-world generator as the held-out domain. Five harness arms, 3 seeds each (about 12-15 agentic RL runs): (a) frozen harness; (b) memory-only adaptive; (c) memory + reflective self-edit, always on; (d) arm (c) fired only on all-fail groups, Harness-S-style; (e) arm (c) plus DAPO dynamic sampling or BAR, to equalize ΔI and isolate the context-conditional-learning residual. A further control arm samples rollouts harness-on but re-scores them harness-free with importance correction (per 2610.02846), which separates what gets sampled from what context the gradient is conditioned on. Every final checkpoint is evaluated three ways: harness-free, under foreign harnesses (a ReAct variant and a harness evolved by a different seed), and in-harness. Each step logs the fractions of informative, all-success and all-fail groups on a probe set, both harness-on and harness-free. The harness-free delta is then regressed on ΔI, adaptivity level and rescue fraction. Compute is matched on env steps, policy-gradient tokens and informative-group count, and all three are reported. Pilot: under 1 week and under $100, Qwen3-1.7B, one ALFWorld split, arms (a), (c) and (d), 1 seed; the check is whether the sign flips between (c) and (d). Full budget is about $1.5-2.5k GPU.
dossier.history: This idea exists only in round 2. It started as field-forecast question Q3 (the Baldwin "hiding effect") and became bold idea NONOBV-7. No round-1 candidate, critique or proposal covers it; round 1 only listed Harness-S in LITERATURE.md and the harness-evolution sweep as "distillation of harness gains is crowded". The original claim was monotone: more harness adaptivity means less weight learning, so the ranking flips between with-harness and harness-free evaluation. The skeptical bold-check found two problems. Two papers had already reported hiding as a side result (CODA App. H.7, and HarnessAdapt-RL's near-answer hints). Three papers showed the opposite sign, an assist (Harness-S, HarnessAdapt-RL's evolved tools and hooks, Self-HPO). So the bold-check pivoted the idea to a two-regime law: hiding or assist depends on which failures the harness rescues (mixed groups vs all-fail groups), measured by ΔI. It also added the gated arm (d) and the ΔI-equalized arm (e). The round-2 REPORT ranks it #10 of 11 at 71, "Promising", and calls it the most counterintuitive idea, but notes it needs GPU and agentic RL seeds are noisy. The field forecast lists it as #4 of the non-obvious picks.
dossier.priorScores: R1: not scored (idea did not exist). R2: forecast Q3 / bold idea NONOBV-7 unscored → bold-check ~72.5 raw, rounded down to ~71 for execution risk (N 3.5, S 4, R 3.5, C 3.5, F 3, T 4.5); REPORT rank #10 at 71, "Promising".

closestPapers.title: Evolving Together, Failing Apart: The Skill-Policy Co-evolution Trap in Self-Improving Agents (CODA)
closestPapers.summary: Argues that the cooperative acceptance rule shared by skill-policy co-evolution methods ties the policy's competence to the skill bank it trained with. Sensitivity to skill drift grows as co-evolution proceeds, and the paper introduces the CO-evolution Drift Audit (CODA) to measure this. Per the bold-check's deep read, App. H.7 reports that the co-evolved ALFWorld policy with its bank removed scores 57.6%, versus 70.6% for a never-skilled pure-RL policy, and the authors describe this as 'standalone ability traded away'.
closestPapers.relation: This is the closest prior on the phenomenon, since it states the hiding effect in words. But it is a single-setting, single-seed side observation that is not compute-matched, has no adaptivity dose, mechanism or foreign-harness evaluation, and covers skill banks only. It rules out 'we discover hiding' as a headline. Our paper has to be the controlled, mechanistic version and must cite H.7 prominently. The authors could also fast-follow.

closestPapers.title: Training the Whole Agent, Not Just the Model (HarnessAdapt-RL)
closestPapers.summary: Trains a 9B coding policy with GRPO while adapting its harness: a frozen teacher supplies mechanism-level skills, and a teacher evolves tools and hooks, accepting each change only if it raises the pass rate or the trainable rate without lowering either. It beats GRPO by 6-13 pp on SWE-bench variants. Gains from mechanism-level skills persist after the skills are removed, while removing the evolved tools and hooks at deployment costs up to 7.7 pp. Per the bold-check, the near-answer-hint variant ends below plain GRPO once hints are removed (32.7 vs 35.3), which the authors attribute to fewer mixed groups (39.0% vs 46.5%).
closestPapers.relation: This is the closest prior on the mechanism, with evidence for both signs: hints cause hiding through contrast collapse, while skills and co-evolved tools show no hiding under the seed harness. That contradicts the original 'adaptivity is the dose' claim and supports the ΔI version. It is one run per configuration, it uses a trainable-rate acceptance gate that guards against hiding, and it is never framed as a law or dose-response.

closestPapers.title: Harness-S: Learning from Sibling Harnesses for Generalizable Agent Training
closestPapers.summary: Evolves specialized sibling harnesses from a common base into a fixed pool, then invokes the pool to rescue failures of the base system during policy training. The goal is a single policy that stays effective under the original harness. Per the bold-check, rescues are injected only when all 8 base rollouts fail, which beats GRPO under H0 (4B AppWorld: 56.9 vs 49.0). Always-on mixed-harness GRPO does worse than plain GRPO (46.7 vs 49.0).
closestPapers.relation: Its gated rescue vs always-on contrast is the two-regime law in miniature, and arm (d) copies its gating. But the paper does not name, sweep or explain the crossover, does not measure ΔI, and its harness pool is fixed rather than self-improving.

closestPapers.title: Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization (Self-HPO)
closestPapers.summary: A recursive framework that alternates harness optimization, in which the current policy analyzes its own failures and proposes harness candidates, with RL on the policy under the selected harness. Hard tasks from training seed the next harness search. Per the bold-check, the policy trained under evolving harnesses scores 64.4 under the seed harness, versus 61.0 for the base policy, using BAR (reward-balanced groups).
closestPapers.relation: A third data point for the assist sign under an adaptive harness, probably because BAR removes zero-variance groups and so suppresses hiding. That is the same mechanism arm (e) tests. It does not compare against a policy trained under a frozen harness and evaluated harness-free.

closestPapers.title: Harness Annealing: Learning to Act with Less External Control
closestPapers.summary: Frames 'harness internalization' as learning to take over a harness's control decisions (what to investigate, whether to revise, when to stop) so that performance survives when support is withdrawn. Its Harness Annealing Training (HAT) combines explicit control supervision with a curriculum over teacher trajectories collected under progressively weaker harnesses. Per the bold-check, plain SFT on harness trajectories collapses without the harness (9B SWE-QA: 16.5 vs 59.9 for base).
closestPapers.relation: Shows that the context-conditional-learning channel of hiding exists apart from group contrast, but through SFT rather than RL. It motivates the arm (e) residual and the re-scoring control. Its curriculum fix is a competitor to the 'gate on all-fail groups' design rule.

closestPapers.title: Understanding Enrichment in Reinforcement Learning
closestPapers.summary: Shows that hint-enriched rollouts in RLVR, when left uncorrected or with truncated importance weights, implicitly reweight the reward. It decomposes the resulting gradient error into scale, rotation and variance, and proposes a sequential Monte Carlo weight correction that keeps correction variance additive rather than exponential. Per the bold-check, enrichment helps in sparse regimes by preventing collapse.
closestPapers.relation: This is the theory hook. Help that rotates the gradient toward successes the base policy cannot produce acts as an assist, and help that up-weights successes the policy already produces acts as hiding. It also supplies the importance-corrected re-scoring control. It is a foundation and methodology source, not a competitor.

closestPapers.title: Multi-Harness Reinforcement Learning for Coding Agents: Training Gains and Harness Dependence
closestPapers.summary: A controlled study that trains two Qwen3-8B RL variants from the same SFT checkpoint on identical replay data. They differ only in whether rewards are normalized within each harness or across harnesses, and both are compared across harnesses on SWE-bench Verified. Per the bold-check, harness-to-harness variance (about 7 pp) exceeds the RL gains (under 1 pp).
closestPapers.relation: Context for the foreign-harness evaluation and for harness dependence of RL gains. It does not vary harness adaptivity or help placement, and it says nothing about hiding.

closestPapers.title: How Learning Can Guide Evolution (Hinton & Nowlan)
closestPapers.summary: The classic simulation of the Baldwin effect: lifetime learning (plasticity) smooths a needle-in-a-haystack fitness landscape, so selection can find and eventually hard-code the good configuration. S2 has no abstract for it, so this summary is from the paper's known content.
closestPapers.relation: The biological foundation. It is the assist side of the Baldwin effect, and the 'hiding effect' (plasticity shielding genotypes from selection) is its counterpart. The bold-check found that no LLM paper uses the Baldwin or hiding framing.

feedback.point: No K1 scoop: no paper treats harness adaptivity as a dose and measures harness-free weight quality at matched rollouts. Nine search channels found no LLM paper with the Baldwin or hiding framing.
feedback.addressed: Positive finding. It supports keeping the Baldwin framing and the controlled-sweep contribution.

feedback.point: The headline phenomenon was already observed as side results, in CODA App. H.7 (co-evolved skill banks; 57.6% vs 70.6% harness-free) and in HarnessAdapt-RL (near-answer hints). 'We discover co-evolution hurts standalone weights' cannot be the headline.
feedback.addressed: Yes. Reframed as the controlled, multi-seed, mechanistic version, and H.7 must be cited prominently.

feedback.point: The opposite sign, a Baldwin assist, has been shown three times (Harness-S all-fail rescue, HarnessAdapt-RL evolved tools and hooks, Self-HPO with BAR). So 'adaptive harness ⇒ hiding' is likely false as a universal claim.
feedback.addressed: Yes. Pivoted to a two-regime law: where the harness helps (mixed vs all-fail groups, ΔI) sets the sign, not adaptivity.

feedback.point: A reviewer will call the rescue-fraction → deficit regression near-tautological: 'rescued groups go all-success and give zero advantage; use DAPO dynamic sampling.'
feedback.addressed: Partly. ΔI is made the explicit measured predictor, and arm (e) equalizes ΔI with dynamic sampling or BAR to isolate context-conditional learning. If (e) removes all hiding, the paper shrinks to 'hiding is a contrast artifact plus a fix' (scored about 65).

feedback.point: The design needs a predicted crossover under the same harness, a decomposition into contrast starvation vs context-conditional learning, and foreign-harness evaluation.
feedback.addressed: Yes. Added gated arm (d), ΔI-equalized arm (e), an importance-corrected harness-free re-scoring control, and foreign-harness evaluation.

feedback.point: Compute matching is subtle: match env steps, policy-gradient tokens and informative-group count, and report all three. The original design said only 'matched rollouts and steps'.
feedback.addressed: Yes, in the revised design.

feedback.point: Agentic RL seed variance is large: CODA's pure-RL baseline swung from 87.5% to 53.1% within 25 steps.
feedback.addressed: Partly. Mitigation is last-k-checkpoint averaging, a pre-registered evaluation step and 3 seeds. Power is still a concern.

feedback.point: Fast-follow risk: CODA's authors (Alibaba) or the HarnessAdapt-RL group could run this, since H.7 explicitly gestures at it. The pilot should be out by January 2027.
feedback.addressed: Not yet; this is a scheduling item.

feedback.point: Mentor relevance is good (a self-improving outer loop vs inner weight learning, the Gödel-Agent question pushed down to weights) but it is less about world models.
feedback.addressed: Not addressed; inherent to the topic.

feedback.point: Ranked #10 at 71 ('Promising'). The most counterintuitive idea, but it needs a GPU and agentic RL seeds are noisy. Scoop risk is low-medium.
feedback.addressed: Acknowledged. The cheap pilot (under $100) is meant to de-risk before the full GPU spend.

feedback.point: The forecast expects biology lenses to stay metaphorical (75% confidence), so few groups will test Baldwin predictions quantitatively. That makes this a low-scoop zone. Original framing: co-evolution papers (Evo², CoEvo-RSI, HPO) never measure harness-ablated weights.
feedback.addressed: Supports the framing. The bold-check later found that Self-HPO and HarnessAdapt-RL do report some harness-ablated numbers, which is what prompted the pivot.

openRisks: Arm (e) may remove all hiding, which would show it is purely a zero-advantage contrast artifact. The paper would then shrink to a known fix (dynamic sampling), at about 65.
Seed variance in agentic RL (swings of 30+ pp) may swamp a ±3 pp effect with 3 seeds; power is unverified.
Fast-follow by the CODA or HarnessAdapt-RL authors before a preprint (target: pilot by Jan 2027).
GPU-bound: 12-15 agentic GRPO runs at up to 40 H100-hours each. The $1.5-2.5k budget is tight if runs overrun.
Matching compute across arms on three axes at once (env steps, gradient tokens, informative groups) may not be achievable, and reviewers may say it is mis-specified.
Less fit with the mentor's world-model agenda; it fits mainly through long-horizon self-improvement and harness robustness.
Several data points used to motivate the law (HarnessAdapt-RL, Self-HPO, CODA H.7) are single-seed preprint results that may not replicate.
OpenReview / ICLR 2027 submissions were not checked (host unreachable); re-check after Dec 4.

judges.strongest: The design tests a predicted sign crossover under one fixed harness. Always-on rescue of mixed groups should cause hiding, and rescue gated to all-fail groups should cause an assist, so the harness is held constant while only where it helps changes. ΔI is the one pre-registered predictor, and the comparison is checked harness-free and under foreign harnesses. Arm (e), which equalizes ΔI, and the importance-corrected re-scoring control are the right tools for separating contrast starvation from context-conditional learning. The pilot is cheap (under $100, about one week) and should show the sign flip quickly.
judges.weakest:
Most of the novelty is already taken.
- TAME (ICLR 2027 submission, openreview IXnpSW8g3v) crosses training and deployment harnesses, measures "capability retained after support removal", and reports "harness rank reversal", where a stronger training harness gives weaker weights. That is the hiding effect with a proper design, and TAME also has a learned fix.
- Harness Annealing (HOk367J7I0) owns harness dependence after training, plus a fix.
- AutoScaffold (KPRr8wWiqO) shows an adaptive scaffold during RL giving a harness-free gain of 7.2 on ALFWorld, our own benchmark. That is the assist pole.
- The mechanism is pre-figured too. HarnessAdapt-RL already attributes hiding to fewer mixed groups (39.0% vs 46.5%), and Harness-S already contrasts all-fail-gated rescue with always-on (56.9 vs 46.7).

What remains is a consolidation: an ΔI regression across 5 arms. That risks K4, because it combines the HarnessAdapt mechanism with the Harness-S gating. A trivially predicted outcome also threatens it: zero-variance groups give zero advantage, so a reviewer will say "of course ΔI predicts it".

Power is poor. There are 3 seeds against agentic-RL swings of 30+ pp, and the effect target is 3 pp. The R² ≥ 0.6 regression rests on about 15 noisy points. If arm (e) removes all hiding, the paper collapses to "use DAPO dynamic sampling".
judges.mustFix:
1. Reposition against the ICLR 2027 submissions, not only the arXiv ones.
   - Cite TAME (IXnpSW8g3v) as owning the hiding and rank-reversal diagnostic, and AutoScaffold (KPRr8wWiqO) as owning adaptive-scaffold assist on ALFWorld. Also cite Harness Annealing (HOk367J7I0), harness entanglement (l8aeyLANkN), One Policy Many Harnesses (4KSNZln9nS) and CODA (ZIBdUe2hGK).
   - Drop "Baldwin hiding" as the headline. The claim must become: ΔI, not harness strength or adaptivity, explains TAME's rank reversal and AutoScaffold's assist.
   - Ideally, show ΔI predicting the sign in a re-implementation of TAME-style and AutoScaffold-style harness conditions, not only in your own arms.
2. Make the ΔI law non-tautological.
   - Pre-register out-of-sample predictions: fit ΔI on ALFWorld and predict the sign and size on TextCraft and τ-world.
   - Make arm (e) and the re-scoring control produce a quantified residual for context-conditional learning, so that either result is a finding.
3. Fix statistical power.
   - Run a seed-variance pilot first.
   - Use at least 5 seeds for the arms on which the crossover depends, (a), (c) and (d).
   - Average over the last k checkpoints, and run TOST with the power analysis reported.
   - Cut arm (b) if needed to fit the budget.
4. Add a second model family (for example Llama or another non-Qwen open model) for the crossover cells only.
5. Run the pilot before December and post a preprint fast, given how many ICLR 2027 submissions now cover this space.
judges.reviewerQuote: TAME already shows harness rank reversal after support removal, AutoScaffold already shows the assist, and Harness-S and HarnessAdapt-RL already show the gated-vs-always-on contrast and the mixed-group explanation, so the remaining contribution is a 3-seed regression of a quantity (informative-group fraction) whose link to GRPO's zero-advantage groups is close to definitional.

judges.strongest: The design cleanly tests whether where the harness helps (mixed vs all-fail groups) or how much it adapts sets the sign. Arm (c) vs (d) uses the same harness and predicts a sign flip. Arm (e) equalizes ΔI and the importance-corrected re-scoring control separates sampling from conditioning context, so the decomposition into contrast starvation vs context-conditional learning is a real mechanistic test that none of the cited papers runs.
judges.weakest: The novelty has collapsed from both sides. On hiding, ICLR 2027's TAME (openreview IXnpSW8g3v) already defines "capability retained after support removal" and "harness rank reversal" (a stronger training harness gives weaker weights) and trains a reviser to fix it. Harness Annealing (HOk367J7I0), Cross-Harness SFT entanglement (l8aeyLANkN, -9.8pp) and One Policy Many Harnesses (4KSNZln9nS) surround it. On assist, AutoScaffold (KPRr8wWiqO, +7.2 ALFWorld harness-free with adaptive scaffolds) and Harness-S already show it, on the same benchmark. A wave of Oct 2026 arXiv papers on rescuing all-fail groups (Grounding Hindsight 2610.21018, VH-GPO 2610.14000, joint decoding 2610.36849, ridge-tracking for mixed groups 2610.25330) makes "help on all-fail groups assists" standard GRPO folklore. "Help that collapses mixed groups into all-success groups removes advantage" is near-tautological under GRPO, the DAPO argument. So the ΔI law mostly restates the zero-variance-group mechanism, and the likely result of arm (e) (hiding vanishes) yields a known fix. Three seeds of agentic GRPO on ALFWorld, where swings of 30 pp are documented, are underpowered for a ±3 pp TOST. 12-15 runs at up to 40 H100-hours each do not fit in $2.5k for a solo undergraduate.
judges.mustFix: Cite TAME (IXnpSW8g3v) and AutoScaffold (KPRr8wWiqO) as the two poles, plus Harness Annealing, l8aeyLANkN, 4KSNZln9nS and the all-fail-rescue GRPO wave (2610.21018, 2610.14000, 2610.36849). Drop "hiding" and "assist" as findings. The only defensible headline is the arm (e) / re-scoring residual: hiding that survives at equal ΔI, meaning context-conditional learning beyond contrast starvation, shown under RL rather than SFT. Pre-register that outcome as the main claim, and present a power analysis from the pilot's seed variance (likely needing 5+ seeds or evaluation averaged over the last k checkpoints) before any GPU spend. Otherwise fold this in as a mechanism analysis section of a broader harness-weights paper, or reproduce TAME's rank reversal and explain it with ΔI.
judges.reviewerQuote: TAME already established harness rank reversal and AutoScaffold and Harness-S already established scaffold assist, and the proposed ΔI "law" is just the well-known fact that zero-variance GRPO groups carry no gradient, so I fail to see what new understanding this 3-seed ALFWorld study adds beyond confirming DAPO's dynamic-sampling rationale.

judges.strongest: This is the only design I know of that holds the harness fixed and changes only where it helps (always-on vs all-fail-gated), then predicts the sign of the harness-free delta from one measured quantity, ΔI. Arm (e), the ΔI-equalized arm, and the importance-corrected re-scoring control together split the effect into contrast starvation and context-conditional learning. That gives a clean causal two-regime story with a usable design rule (gate help on all-fail groups).
judges.weakest: The space is now saturated. The ICLR 2027 sweep (Nov 12) found TAME (openreview IXnpSW8g3v, rated scoop/high). TAME already defines "capability retained after support removal" and "harness rank reversal" (a stronger training harness yields weaker weights), and it trains an agent to revise the training harness for transfer. Around TAME sit five more papers: Harness Annealing (HOk367J7I0), which covers dependence plus a fix; AutoScaffold (KPRr8wWiqO), which shows assist with +7.2 harness-free on ALFWorld, the same benchmark we use; One Policy, Many Harnesses (4KSNZln9nS); harness entanglement (l8aeyLANkN), which covers the foreign-harness readout; and competence-adaptive release (vMD5ZXhd2P). Add the arXiv set (CODA H.7, HarnessAdapt-RL, Harness-S, Self-HPO), and both signs and the gating trick are already published. What remains, "ΔI predicts the sign", reads as the known zero-advantage-group effect from DAPO and dynamic sampling. Arm (e) could reduce the paper to that known fix. On top of this, 3 seeds of agentic GRPO with 30-pp swings is badly underpowered for a ±3 pp claim and an R² ≥ 0.6 regression across only about 5 arm-level points.
judges.mustFix: 1. Position against TAME (IXnpSW8g3v) as the primary prior, not CODA H.7, and explicitly give up "hiding" and "rank reversal" as contributions. The headline has to be only the ΔI placement law plus the decomposition: how much of the effect survives ΔI equalization in arm (e). Pre-register what happens if that residual is about 0. 2. Cite and differentiate Harness Annealing, AutoScaffold (same ALFWorld setting), l8aeyLANkN, 4KSNZln9nS, cCqHNd56Pp, vMD5ZXhd2P, TrackRL, FPaMYO47j4 and Harness-Zero. 3. Change the regression from arm-level to group-level or step-level ΔI data. Use a continuous gating threshold (fire when the success rate is ≤ k/8, sweeping k) so the law has many dose points rather than 5 arms. 4. Run a power analysis from the pilot's seed variance before the full spend. That likely means fewer arms and more seeds (at least 5), on TextCraft or ALFWorld only. 5. Ship the pilot by January 2027. Proceed only if the (c) vs (d) sign flip is larger than the seed spread at 1.7B.
judges.reviewerQuote: Hiding and assist are already documented by TAME, AutoScaffold and Harness-S, and the proposed ΔI "law" largely restates that all-success GRPO groups carry zero advantage, which DAPO's dynamic sampling already addresses, so the contribution reduces to a noisy three-seed confirmation of a known mechanism.

dossier.title: Same Teacher, Different Learner: Is Task Value Learner-Relative Across Weight and Harness Substrates? (teacher-substrate, C12; parked in round 1)
dossier.claim: Latest version, the round-1 critique's sharpened claim; no later version exists. Task value depends on the learner. For gradient learners, a task's training value is predicted by outcome variance. For reflective harness learners, it is predicted by coverage of unresolved, attributable failure rules. So pass-rate-frontier teachers lose most of their advantage when moved from LoRA-GRPO to GEPA/ACE, while rule-coverage teachers transfer in both directions (asymmetric transfer, not a symmetric flip). The original C12 claim was a symmetric ranking flip: frontier and learning-progress (LP) teachers best for GRPO but among the worst for harness learners.
dossier.design:
Original C12 design:
- 5 named teachers (random, frontier band, LP bandit, hint-regret, coverage ledger) x 2 learners (a harness on a frozen 8B model vs LoRA-GRPO on the same 8B).
- Matched teacher compute, 5 seeds, about $500 API plus 200–400 GPU-hours.

Critique-recommended revision, never written up as a proposal:
- Factorize the teachers: ranking signal (pass-rate frontier / LP / coverage gain) x ranking unit (task vs rule or failure pattern). Include an ActiveSaddler-style failure-pattern LP arm.
- Add a third substrate: GEPA prompt, ACE/DAEDALUS-style memory, and LoRA-GRPO weights.
- Use a procedural hidden-rule environment where coverage is measured exactly and held-out tasks are unlimited. Keep one real benchmark (τ²-retail or AppWorld) as an external-validity check.
- Define a per-task, per-learner informativeness: reward variance or advantage norm for GRPO; the probability of an accepted, attributable edit for harness learners. Test whether it predicts teacher rankings.
- Report budget curves at 2–3 budget levels.
- Add a teacher-transfer regret test: tune on substrate A, deploy on B.
- Run a pilot under $50 for a power analysis, and preregister asymmetric transfer.
dossier.history: Round 1: C12 was generated as a new topic-T4 candidate. The adversarial critique scored it 62.1 ("viable only with fixes") and the round-1 REPORT parked it at rank 16 of 19. The critique recommended reframing it from a "ranking flip" to "learner-relative task value with a predictive quantity", and folding it into Dan's lead #3 (curriculum-goodhart) as a section or ablation rather than a standalone paper. The round-1 curriculum-goodhart proposal did absorb a harness-vs-LoRA substrate contrast (a 2×2 of {harness, weight learner} x {frozen, self-edited writer}). In round 2, curriculum-goodhart v2 explicitly dropped the weight-vs-harness 2×2 and cut the weight arm, calling it "the weight result moved onto a new substrate" and cheap to scoop. So no descendant of teacher-substrate survives into round 2. It received no round-2 red-team, bold-check or proposal. Round-2 field_forecast labels self-generated envs and curricula "saturated for methods".
dossier.priorScores: R1 critique 62.1 (N 3.0, S 3.5, R 2.5, C 3.0, F 3.0, T 4.0) → parked (round-1 REPORT rank 16). Not scored in R2. Critique's estimate with fixes 1–3: about 70–72. Mock-review decision: borderline reject (4/10) as specified; could reach weak accept (6) with a preregistered interaction, a mechanism and at least 2 environments.

closestPapers.title: ActiveSaddler: Automated Curriculum Learning for Agent Harness Optimization
closestPapers.summary: Frames choosing which training scenarios drive harness updates as automated curriculum learning. A non-stationary bandit runs over LLM-abstracted failure-pattern arms, prioritized by estimated learning progress, with explicit exploration of unseen scenarios. Improves test Pass@1 by 4.4 pp (GAIA2) and 7.5 pp (Terminal-Bench 2.0) over the same optimizer with a fixed scenario order. Ablations show the gains depend on dynamically built targets and utility estimates.
closestPapers.relation: Directly tests curricula for harness learners, but harness-only with no gradient learner. Its winning teacher is an LP bandit, which contradicts C12's prediction that LP is among the worst teachers for harnesses. Per the round-1 critique, the arm unit (failure pattern vs scenario or category) swings results by 3–11 pp, so any substrate 'flip' could be an arm-granularity artifact. This is why the critique asks to factorize ranking signal x ranking unit.

closestPapers.title: GEPA-Curator: Curated Learning for Self Improving Agents
closestPapers.summary: Argues that many agentic failures (harness limits, stochasticity, noisy judges) give reflective prompt optimizers like GEPA no useful signal, or even harmful signal. It adds task curation, which filters out unreliable tasks, and prior-success retrieval, which feeds past successful trajectories to the optimizer. Gains of up to 20.7% over GEPA and 21.2% over ACE on GoBrowse, ALFWorld, AppWorld and τ-bench.
closestPapers.relation: Supplies the mechanism half of C12 for harness learners: per the critique's deep read, a numerical success/failure curriculum underperforms vanilla GEPA (62.5 vs 66.2), and contrastive success/failure pairs help. It never runs a weight learner or a teacher x substrate factorial. Its notion of 'frontier' is a qualitative LLM judgment.

closestPapers.title: GRADUS: Discovering and Recovering Agent Lessons from the Environment's Latent Syllabus
closestPapers.summary: Treats a policy-constrained tool environment as a latent syllabus. It extracts guarded behavioral operators, composes them into harder tasks, and uses corpus-level feedback to target missing outcome combinations, calibrating tasks and solutions jointly against the environment. The resulting curriculum lifts a 30B model from 59% to 89% on τ²-Bench and from 47% to 83% on CAR-Bench.
closestPapers.relation: This is the coverage-ledger teacher, and it wins for a gradient learner (SFT+GRPO). Per the critique, removing the ledger costs up to 21 pp. That undercuts the 'coverage for harnesses, frontier for weights' split and motivated the switch to an asymmetric-transfer prediction. Weights only; no harness learner.
